sources.title: Syncing manual game-test logs from my phone into Sheets — trigger keeps failing
sources.text: I have tried a Schedule Trigger plus Google Drive Watch Files and also a Webhook from a shortcut on the phone, but the workflow either doesn’t fire at all or fires twice on the same file.
taskExcerpts: I have tried a Schedule Trigger plus Google Drive Watch Files and also a Webhook from a shortcut on the phone, but the workflow either doesn’t fire at all or fires twice on the same file.

spans.text: I test mobile games on a couple of phones and keep a simple log while I play: battery percentage, device temperature, frame drops, and a short note about what I was doing when it happened. Right now I type it into a notes app during the session, then later export a CSV from that app and paste it into a Google Sheet. It works, but I only remember to do it at the end of the day.
I have tried a Schedule Trigger plus Google Drive Watch Files and also a Webhook from a shortcut on the phone, but the workflow either doesn’t fire at all or fires twice on the same file.

I’m not sure whether the problem is the trigger watching the wrong folder, the phone not finishing the upload before the workflow reads it, or my CSV parsing. Has anyone automated a similar phone-to-Sheets flow with n8n? I’d like to know what trigger you use and how you stop it from grabbing the same file twice. I’m on the free community edition for now.

spans.text: How to keep useful workflow automation while moving core logistics logic into reliable software
A simple flow can notify a dispatcher when a shipment is delayed, copy an order update into a CRM, alert a buyer when inventory drops, or send a daily report to a team channel.
Workflow automation is often a strong fit for event-driven tasks with clear inputs and outputs. Examples include:

n8n can remain valuable after a logistics company adopts custom software. It is well suited to many integrations, notifications, and orchestration tasks. It becomes risky when critical business rules, transaction state, and operational permissions are scattered across flows without a clear source of truth. Map the current workflows, classify them by business risk, and move one critical process at a time. A good logistics software development partner will help preserve what works, strengthen the underlying architecture, and make the transition measurable.
